name: Okinawa
tagline: A subtropical island chain with its own Ryukyu Kingdom history, distinct food and language, and coral reefs that feel like a different country from mainland Japan entirely.
highlight: Cape Manzamo's dramatic elephant-trunk-shaped cliff, dropping into brilliant turquoise water along Okinawa's western coast.
shortDescription: Japan's subtropical southern islands, their own Ryukyu Kingdom history, coral reefs and distinct food culture setting them apart from the mainland.
metaDescription: An Okinawa travel guide: Shurijo Castle, the Churaumi Aquarium, coral reef beaches, when to go and a practical five-day itinerary.
knownFor: Coral reef beaches, Ryukyu Kingdom history, distinct cuisine
goodFor: Beaches, snorkelling, history, a different pace of Japan

image.alt: Cape Manzamo's dramatic cliff dropping into turquoise water on Okinawa's coast

intro: Okinawa was, until 1879, an independent kingdom — the Ryukyu Kingdom — with its own language, distinct culture and centuries of trade relationships across East and Southeast Asia, and that separate history still shapes the islands' identity within modern Japan. Annexed relatively late and devastated by one of the Pacific War's bloodiest ground battles, Okinawa's relationship with the rest of the country remains visibly its own.

The islands' subtropical climate and coral reefs offer a different Japan from the mainland's temperate cities and mountains — turquoise water, white sand beaches and some of the country's best diving and snorkelling, alongside a slower, warmer pace of daily life often summed up in the local phrase 'Okinawa time'.

Food, language and even burial customs still carry distinct Ryukyuan influence, and Okinawa's reputation for longevity — among the world's most-studied populations for exceptional lifespan — is tied to this separate culture, its diet and its community structure rather than being simply a warmer version of mainland Japanese life.

whyVisit.intro: Okinawa's case is that no other part of Japan carries this distinct a separate history, culture and coral-reef landscape.

points.title: The Ryukyu Kingdom history is distinct
points.text: Centuries as an independent kingdom left a language, culture and architecture separate from mainland Japan.

points.title: The coral reefs are excellent
points.text: Among Japan's best diving and snorkelling, with visibility and marine life that rival far more famous tropical destinations.

points.title: The food culture is its own
points.text: Distinct dishes and ingredients set Okinawan cuisine clearly apart from anything found on the mainland.

points.title: The history is sobering and important
points.text: The Battle of Okinawa's memorial sites offer essential context for understanding the islands' modern identity.

points.title: The pace is different
points.text: A slower, warmer island rhythm offers real contrast to mainland Japan's more famously fast-paced cities.

attractionsIntro: Okinawa's essential sights, spanning its royal Ryukyu Kingdom history and its dramatic coastline.

attractions.name: Shurijo Castle

image.file: File:View of Shureimon (Winuaijo) Gate of Shuri Castle.JPG
image.alt: The Shureimon Gate at Shurijo Castle Park

attractions.text: The former royal palace of the Ryukyu Kingdom, a UNESCO World Heritage site whose distinct red-lacquered architecture reflects centuries of Chinese and Japanese cultural exchange.
attractions.tip: The castle's main hall was destroyed by fire in 2019 and remains under reconstruction — check current visitor access before planning around it.

attractions.name: Churaumi Aquarium

image.file: File:Whale Shark - Churaumi aquarium, Okinawa, Japan.jpg
image.alt: A whale shark in the Churaumi Aquarium's main tank

attractions.text: One of the world's largest aquariums, its enormous main tank home to whale sharks and manta rays, a spectacular centrepiece of the Okinawa Churaumi Marine Park.
attractions.tip: Arrive near feeding times, posted at the entrance, for the most active viewing of the main tank's largest residents.

attractions.name: Cape Manzamo
attractions.text: A dramatic elephant-trunk-shaped cliff formation dropping into brilliant turquoise water, one of Okinawa's most photographed natural landmarks.
attractions.tip: The short coastal walking path around the cape offers several striking angles beyond the main viewpoint.

attractions.name: Kokusai-dori, Naha

image.alt: Kokusai-dori, Naha's main shopping and dining street

attractions.text: Naha's main shopping and dining street, lively with local crafts, Okinawan food stalls and a covered arcade market just off its length.
attractions.tip: The Makishi Public Market, just off Kokusai-dori, offers a more local, less touristy food experience.

attractions.name: Kabira Bay, Ishigaki

image.alt: Kabira Bay's turquoise water and small islands on Ishigaki

attractions.text: A stunning bay of turquoise and deep-blue water dotted with small islands, among the most photographed views in the wider Yaeyama Islands.
attractions.tip: Swimming is restricted in parts of the bay to protect its pearl farms — glass-bottom boat tours are the main way to see it up close.

attractions.name: Peace Memorial Park, Itoman

image.alt: The Cornerstone of Peace Memorial at Okinawa's Peace Memorial Park

attractions.text: A moving memorial to the Battle of Okinawa, one of the Pacific War's bloodiest ground battles, listing the names of all who died regardless of nationality.
attractions.tip: The adjacent Okinawa Prefectural Peace Memorial Museum provides essential context for the park's memorials.

thingsToDoIntro: Beyond the historic sites, Okinawa rewards its coral reefs, its distinct culture and its different island pace.

thingsToDo.title: Snorkel or dive Okinawa's coral reefs

image.file: File:Shimajirizaki and Kerama Islands seen from Tonaki Island 202407.jpg
image.alt: The Kerama Islands, a top diving and snorkelling destination off Okinawa

thingsToDo.text: Excellent visibility and reef health make Okinawa one of Japan's best diving and snorkelling destinations, rivalling far more famous tropical spots.
thingsToDo.tip: The Kerama Islands, a short boat trip from Naha, offer some of the clearest water and healthiest reefs in the region.

thingsToDo.title: Relax on a beach in Miyako or Ishigaki

image.alt: White sand and turquoise water on a Miyako Island beach

thingsToDo.text: The outer islands hold some of Japan's best beaches, with white sand and consistently clear turquoise water.
thingsToDo.tip: Miyako's Yonaha Maehama Beach is regularly ranked among Japan's best, with a long, uncrowded stretch of sand.

thingsToDo.title: Visit a traditional Ryukyuan village

image.file: File:Interior of a traditional home in Ryukyu Mura.jpg
image.alt: The interior of a traditional Ryukyuan home at Ryukyu Mura

thingsToDo.text: Recreated historic villages offer genuine insight into pre-annexation Ryukyu Kingdom architecture, crafts and daily life.
thingsToDo.tip: Ryukyu Mura combines traditional buildings with craft demonstrations, a good introduction before visiting Shurijo Castle.

thingsToDo.title: Learn about Okinawan karate's roots

image.alt: Karate practice at an Okinawan dojo

thingsToDo.text: Modern karate originated in Okinawa, developed from indigenous fighting traditions and Chinese martial arts exchange.
thingsToDo.tip: Several dojos across the islands offer visitor-friendly introductory sessions, a hands-on way to engage with the history.

thingsToDo.title: Eat Okinawa soba for lunch

image.alt: A bowl of Okinawa soba at a local restaurant

thingsToDo.text: A different noodle from mainland soba, made with wheat rather than buckwheat, in a pork-based broth, an everyday island staple.
thingsToDo.tip: Look for small family-run soba shops away from Kokusai-dori for a more authentic, less tourist-priced bowl.

thingsToDo.title: Try awamori at a local bar

image.file: File:Awamori by Blue Lotus in Okinawa.jpg
image.alt: A glass of awamori, Okinawa's own distilled spirit

thingsToDo.text: Okinawa's own distilled spirit, made from long-grain rice using a technique distinct from mainland sake or shochu production, a genuine local specialty.
thingsToDo.tip: Aged awamori (kusu) is smoother and more complex than younger versions — worth the modest price difference.

foodIntro: Okinawan food stands apart from the mainland, shaped by the islands' distinct history, climate and Ryukyu Kingdom trade connections.

foods.name: Okinawa soba

image.file: File:Okinawa soba noodles with deeply cooked pork (6059482310).jpg
image.alt: Okinawa soba topped with stewed pork belly

foods.text: Wheat noodles in a pork-based broth, topped with stewed pork belly, distinct from mainland buckwheat soba despite the shared name.
foods.whereToTry: Family-run soba shops throughout the islands, an everyday local staple rather than a special-occasion dish.

foods.name: Goya champuru

image.alt: Goya champuru, a stir-fry of bitter melon, tofu, egg and pork

foods.text: A stir-fry of bitter melon, tofu, egg and pork, a genuine Okinawan comfort food built around an ingredient the islands are particularly known for.
foods.whereToTry: Traditional Okinawan restaurants (izakaya) throughout Naha and the outer islands.

foods.name: Rafute

image.file: File:Rafti, Okinawan stewed pork belly by Blue Lotus.jpg
image.alt: Rafute, pork belly slow-braised in awamori, soy sauce and brown sugar

foods.text: Pork belly slow-braised in awamori, soy sauce and brown sugar until tender, a signature dish reflecting Okinawa's historically important pork culture.
foods.whereToTry: Traditional Okinawan restaurants, often served as part of a larger set meal.

foods.name: Awamori

image.alt: A bottle of Kikunotsuyu awamori, Okinawa's distilled rice spirit

foods.text: Okinawa's own distilled rice spirit, made using a distinct black koji fermentation method separate from mainland sake or shochu traditions.
foods.whereToTry: Local bars and dedicated awamori distilleries offering tastings across the islands.

foods.name: Taco rice

image.alt: Taco rice, seasoned taco filling served over rice

foods.text: Seasoned taco filling served over rice rather than a tortilla, a genuine Okinawan invention reflecting decades of American military presence on the islands.
foods.whereToTry: Casual diners throughout Naha, a beloved local comfort food rather than a novelty.

foods.name: Beni-imo (purple sweet potato) sweets

image.alt: A beni-imo purple sweet potato tart

foods.text: Okinawa's distinctive purple sweet potato appears throughout the islands' desserts, tarts and even soft serve, a popular local specialty.
foods.whereToTry: Bakeries and souvenir shops throughout Naha and Kokusai-dori, particularly for the tart known locally as beni-imo tart.

accommodation.intro: Okinawa's accommodation spreads across Naha's city convenience and the outer islands' beach resorts.

areas.name: Naha
areas.text: The main island's capital, with Shurijo Castle, Kokusai-dori and the airport all within easy reach.

areas.name: Onna, on the main island's west coast
areas.text: A popular resort strip putting Cape Manzamo and Churaumi Aquarium within reasonable driving distance.

areas.name: Ishigaki or Miyako
areas.text: A short flight from Naha, these outer islands hold the region's best beaches and reef access.

gettingThere.intro: Naha Airport is Okinawa's main gateway, with domestic flights the practical way to reach the outer islands.

options.text: Well connected to Tokyo, Osaka and other major Japanese cities, with a growing range of direct international routes.
options.detail: Flights from Tokyo take about 2h45, considerably faster than any rail or ferry alternative.

options.mode: Domestic flights to the outer islands
options.text: Short flights connect Naha to Ishigaki and Miyako in under an hour, the practical way to reach the region's best beaches.
options.detail: Book ahead in peak summer season, when outer island flights can sell out.

options.text: Longer, slower ferry connections link Naha to several of the outer islands for those with more time and a preference for sea travel.
options.detail: Ferries are more affordable than flights but take considerably longer, sometimes overnight.

gettingAround.intro: A rental car is the most practical way to explore Okinawa's main island beyond central Naha.

options.text: The most flexible way to reach Cape Manzamo, Churaumi Aquarium and the main island's beaches at your own pace.
options.detail: An International Driving Permit is required, and Okinawa drives on the left, as with the rest of Japan.

options.text: Naha's monorail covers the city centre and airport well, useful for a Naha-focused day or two.
options.detail: Beyond central Naha, the monorail's reach is limited — a car or bus becomes necessary.

options.text: Cover the main island reasonably, though with considerably less frequency and coverage than mainland Japan's urban transit.
options.detail: Routes and schedules can be confusing for first-time visitors — a car remains the more practical option for most itineraries.

bestTime.headline: April–June and October–November, for warm weather without peak humidity or typhoons
bestTime.summary: Okinawa's subtropical climate means warm weather most of the year, with typhoon season and summer humidity the main factors to plan around.

seasons.text: Warm, increasingly clear water and comfortable temperatures before the peak of summer humidity and crowds.
Hot, humid and the peak of typhoon season — check forecasts closely if travelling during these months.
Still warm enough for swimming, with typhoon risk easing and crowds noticeably thinner than summer.
Mild by mainland standards but too cool for most swimming, a good season for sightseeing without crowds.

bestTime.avoid: Peak typhoon season (August–September) without flexible travel plans, when storms can disrupt flights and ferries with little notice.

itinerary.intro: Naha's history and food first, then the main island's coast, with an option to extend to the outer islands.

days.title: Arrive in Naha
days.summary: The city's centre and Ryukyu history.
days.evening: Dinner and a walk along Kokusai-dori.

days.title: Naha's markets and culture
days.evening: An izakaya dinner featuring rafute and goya champuru.

days.title: The west coast
days.evening: Dinner in the Onna resort area.

days.title: Beaches and the Peace Memorial Park
days.morning: The Peace Memorial Park and Museum in Itoman.

days.summary: Ishigaki's Kabira Bay or a direct flight home.
days.morning: Fly to Ishigaki if extending, or depart directly.

tipsIntro: Practical notes on weather, transport and booking that make a real difference to an Okinawa trip.
tips: Check typhoon forecasts closely if travelling in August or September, and keep flight plans flexible during that window.
Rent a car for the main island — public transport beyond central Naha is limited.
Book outer island flights and accommodation ahead in peak summer season, when availability tightens.
Try Okinawa soba at a small family-run shop rather than a Kokusai-dori tourist restaurant for better value and flavour.
Check Shurijo Castle's current reconstruction status before visiting, following the 2019 fire.
Bring reef-safe sunscreen — Okinawa's coral reefs are sensitive to standard sunscreen chemicals.
Allow real travel time between the main island and the outer islands if attempting to combine both in one trip.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Okinawa?
faq.a: Five to six for the main island alone; add two or three more if extending to Ishigaki or Miyako for the region's best beaches and diving.

faq.q: Is Okinawa very different from mainland Japan?
faq.a: Yes — the islands' separate Ryukyu Kingdom history, distinct food culture, subtropical climate and slower pace set Okinawa clearly apart from the mainland experience.

faq.q: Do I need to fly to the outer islands, or can I combine everything on the main island?
faq.a: The main island alone offers worthwhile beaches, history and the aquarium, but the outer islands' best diving and beaches require a short domestic flight.

faq.q: What is the best time of year to visit?
faq.a: April to June and October to November offer warm weather with lower typhoon risk than peak summer, which runs humid with real storm potential.

faq.q: Is Okinawa expensive compared to mainland Japan?
faq.a: Broadly comparable, with domestic flights to the outer islands the main additional cost beyond a typical mainland Japan trip.
